displayQuote: I'm not young enough to know everything

meta.title: Who really said "I'm not young enough to know everything"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Oscar Wilde. J. M. Barrie wrote the line for the dandy Ernest in his 1902 play The Admirable Crichton — a deliberate Wilde parody.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'm not young enough to know everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Oscar Wilde. It's J. M. Barrie's line from The Admirable Crichton (1902), spoken by a character who parodies Wilde's own wit.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — actually J. M. Barrie
answer.authorDates: 1860–1937 · Scottish novelist & playwright, creator of Peter Pan
answer.sourceLine: The line belongs to J. M. Barrie’s comedy The Admirable Crichton (1902), where the aristocratic dandy Ernest delivers it in Act I — and even labours to explain the joke. The character is a deliberate parody of a Wilde-style epigram-monger, which is likely why the quip later drifted onto Wilde himself. Quote Investigator found no evidence Wilde ever wrote or spoke it.

source.heading: The line in Barrie’s play
source.excerpt:
ERNEST: I’m not young enough to know everything.
TREHERNE: How do you mean, Ernest?
ERNEST: I mean what I say.
LADY MARY: Say it again; say it more slowly.
ERNEST: I’m—not—young—enough—to—know—everything.
TREHERNE: I see. What you really mean, my boy, is that you are not old enough to know everything.
ERNEST: No, I don’t.
trail: Quote Investigator credits J. M. Barrie’s The Admirable Crichton and finds no substantive evidence Wilde crafted the quip.
The line appears in Act I of the play, spoken by Ernest and greeted with blank incomprehension.
Wikiquote’s sourced J. M. Barrie section lists it as Ernest’s line from Act I of The Admirable Crichton.
Interesting Literature notes Ernest is a knowing satire of the Wilde-style epigram hero — a clue to how the misattribution grew.
source.excerptNote: Barrie stages the epigram as a dud: Ernest has to repeat it and nobody in the room is impressed — the opposite of a Wilde triumph.

source.rightsNote: The Admirable Crichton was first staged in 1902 and published well before 1931 (it is freely available at Project Gutenberg), so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: J. M. Barrie
author.heading: J. M. Barrie
author.metaLine: 1860–1937 · Scottish novelist & playwright, creator of Peter Pan
author.bio: Sir James Matthew Barrie (1860–1937) was a Scottish dramatist and novelist best known for creating Peter Pan. A contemporary of Oscar Wilde, he was a master of drawing-room comedy; The Admirable Crichton (1902) is among his most admired plays. In it he built the character Ernest partly to lampoon the Wilde-style epigram-dropper — which is why one of Ernest’s lines eventually got mistaken for a genuine Wilde saying.

misattribution.heading: How Wilde got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is genuinely witty and Wildean in flavour, so it reads perfectly as an Oscar Wilde epigram — but the evidence points squarely at J. M. Barrie.

items.why: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Wilde ever wrote or said this; it appears in none of his works. The related line Wilde did publish in 1894 was “The old believe everything: the middle-aged suspect everything: the young know everything” — a different joke.
Per QI, Herbert Prochnow’s 1955 Speaker’s Handbook correctly credited Barrie but printed Wilde’s name nearby; Robert Byrne’s 1986 collection then credited Wilde outright, and the mistake propagated.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Barrie’s, written for a fictional dandy who is himself a send-up of Wilde — confirmed in Act I of The Admirable Crichton.

context.heading: Why the confusion is almost poetic
lead: Barrie wrote Ernest Woolley as a gentle parody of the Wilde-style wit — a young man who manufactures paradoxes and then, comically, has to explain them because no one laughs. The joke of the scene is that the epigram fails.
So the line was designed to sound like Wilde. That it later got filed under Wilde’s name is, in a sense, the parody landing a century late.
context.pull: Barrie wrote the line to sound like Wilde — so of course it ended up credited to him.
